DecSummary: The application of the defendants in a civil case to reconsider Decision No. 437/00 was denied. The vice-chair considered the evidence and came to a reasonable conclusion. The vice-chair did not specifically refer to three pieces of evidence that the defendants alleged were of critical importance. However, the Vice-Chair did not find those pieces of evidence to be important. It is not necessary to refer to all evidence in a decision. Rather, the evidentiary basis for the decision must be clear.

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Resolution Officer regarding his FEL award. In Decision No. 2115/00, the hearing panel dismissed the worker's appeal. The worker applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 2115/00.

The worker had entitlement for chronic pain disability. The worker may have demonstrated exaggerated pain behaviour but that behaviour was consistent honestly motivated either due to fear of pain that might result from physical examination or exertion or because the worker was motivated to make sure the doctor knew the seriousness of the disability. The Vice-Chair was satisfied that the worker experienced genuine pain which was consistent and continuous. Any exaggeration can be accounted for in the assessment of benefits.

The worker's application to reconsider Decisions No. 909/00 and 909/00R was denied. The worker submitted a new medical report. However, the Vice-Chair found that the new report was in the nature of medical advocacy, and did not overturn the existing medical evidence that was discussed and considered in the original decision.

The original vice-chair considered the evidence and law and came to a reasonable conclusion. Evidence of the amount of the worker's NEL award for chronic pain disability did not constitute substantial new evidence, as the issue of chronic pain had been considered at the original hearing, so that the amount of the NEL award was simply more evidence of the same issue.

The worker's application to reconsider Decision No. 1304/00 was denied. There was an unexplained delay of 10 years in bringing the application to reconsider. In any event, new evidence submitted by the worker would not have changed the result of the original decision.

DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in 1994 and an elbow injury in 1997. In Decision No. 3164/00, the Tribunal denied the worker entitlement for fibromyalgia. The worker applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 3164/00, taking issue with the finding that the pain related to the worker's fibromyalgia pre-dated the compensable accidents. The worker submitted a further letter from her doctor to clarify his earlier report concerning the onset of fibromyalgia. In Decision No. 3164/00R, the same vice-chair who made the original decision denied the application for reconsideration. The vice-chair noted that the new letter was written by the doctor after being advised by the worker to clarify his previous report. Even if the new letter could not have been made available at the original hearing, it still failed to satisfy requirements of Board policy regarding marked life disruptions and pain inconsistent with organic findings.

The request did not point to any significant defect in the administrative process or content of the decision that, if corrected, would have altered its outcome, but rather was an attempt to re-argue the appeal.
